Text at the top reads: She said she'd just hop on bareback. I've been standing by the fence for twenty minutes waiting for the hop.
posts.caption: I have a scar on my left knee from the last time I said I'd just hop on bareback. That was 2011, and the horse was a foot shorter. Red is seventeen hands and the only step that works is the mounting block. I dragged it into the paddock this afternoon and carried a cup of coffee out like I had all day. Which I did. Red stood there like a closed bank. By the time I got my leg over, the coffee was cold and my good flannel was a lost cause. She started walking at once, as if none of it had happened.
posts.first: The first time I got on Red I used the tailgate of the truck and a feed bucket. She waited so politely I assumed she was proud of me. Years later I figured out she was just resting. We both got a break and that's all I'll say about it.

posts.caption: The puddle outside the hay shed has been there since last Thursday, and Pudding has walked past it twice a day without a glance. This morning something in him changed. I was carrying a flake of hay to the trough when he stopped dead, ears locked forward, and stared at it like it owed him money. We went the long way around, all forty feet of extra fence line, with him pressed against my hip. I checked the puddle afterward. There was a leaf in it. I haven't told him.
posts.first: Pudding once refused to cross a shadow for a full ten minutes. I stood holding the lead rope in the cold and learned that I am a patient person when I have no other choice. He walked over it eventually, looking very pleased. I have never seen a pony so proud of ignoring a shadow.

posts.quote: The vet's invoice has a line that just says 'misc.' I've decided not to ask what misc did.
posts.first: I keep every vet invoice in a folder labeled Taxes. My husband opened it once and closed it very gently. We haven't discussed it since, and the horse has had a lovely year. I consider that a successful partnership.

posts.caption: He's twenty-six, and the vet says his knees have earned an early retirement, which he's been enjoying since 2019. Every night at nine-thirty I stop at his stall to check the heater on his water bucket. Tonight he was already at the window, nose on the sill, though there wasn't a flake in the sky yet. The forecast said Thursday. He doesn't read forecasts. He just knows. I stood next to him for a few minutes without saying anything, which is how he prefers it. The bucket heater was fine.
posts.first: My first winter with him I spent a hundred dollars on a fancy blanket. He wore it twice and then let it sit in the corner like a nice coat at a party. These days I give him extra hay and a quiet barn. He seems to think that's the better deal.

posts.caption: It took me forty minutes with a wide-tooth comb and a spray bottle of detangler to get my mare's forelock to lie just so. I took one photo for posterity. Then the hood went on, because it dropped to twenty-eight overnight and I'm not a monster. She wore it out to the paddock like she was walking into a gala. She found a puddle with ice on it and placed one hoof on it with great ceremony. It cracked. She looked at me. I said nothing, and neither of us has brought it up.
posts.first: She stood perfectly still for the entire forelock project and then shook her head the second I stepped back. I took it as a review. After eleven years together I've learned to read them.

Headline: The last load of second cutting is here. It's green and it smells like July. Subtitle: I would like to be left alone with it.
posts.caption: The hay guy pulled in at 7:10 with the last load of second cutting, the kind you can smell from the mailbox. I stood in the barn aisle with a cup of coffee and watched him stack two hundred bales to the rafters. By the time he finished, the whole barn smelled like a July afternoon. All twelve horses stood at their doors with their noses in the air. Mine closed her eyes. I had to remind myself it was a delivery and not a miracle. Then I wrote the check and the feeling mostly passed.
posts.first: I keep one flake from every good load in the tack room, sealed in a feed bag, and open it in February when the barn smells like wet wool. It works every time. My husband thinks I'm hoarding. I tell him it's an emergency supply of summer.
